prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, founding the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a discovery in the sense I care about: a quantitative theoretical prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) of a flat band at a specific twist angle, followed seven years later by an experiment in which nature delivered something nobody had demanded of it, namely gate-tunable correlated insulators and superconductivity in a carbon-only system (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018). Theory and experiment are tightly linked, the result has been reproduced by many groups, and it has spawned moire platforms well beyond graphene (twisted TMDs, fractional Chern states, moire excitons). It also has the broadest conceptual reach of the shortlist: a single geometric knob controls band structure and interaction strength. It is the only candidate that four of the first-ranked or second-ranked colleagues (Eriksson, Johansson, Lindroth, and I) all place in their top two, and that is a signal about robustness across different specialisms, though I do not equate it with merit.
statement.case_against: The credited trio leaves out Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 experiments, and Valla Fatemi, and the experimentally decisive work on related moire systems by other groups (Dean, Young, Kim, Ashoori) lies outside the supplied credit list. The three-person limit forces a hard choice that may look unfair to junior experimentalists. The superconducting pairing mechanism is still unsettled, so a citation must be written carefully around the existence of the correlated states and the flat-band platform rather than around an explanation. Finally, a prize this fresh could be judged early compared with the optical clock or ion-trap theory candidates, which have decades of confirmation.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock (B061, Katori and Ye) first as a clean, concrete advance in precision with a natural two-name credit, strong independent confirmation and an unrecognised application of the comb prize.
responses.response: I agree with most of that and I rank B061 second myself. The attribution is cleaner than for moire matter and the maturity is not in doubt. Where I differ is on what is new in nature: the lattice clock is a superb refinement of a measurement we already knew how to make, and its fundamental-physics payoff (redshift, constants) is still prospective, while twisted graphene revealed an entirely new regime of correlated matter. I would not oppose B061 as a fallback, and I would find a clock prize easier to write a citation for, but I do not think ease of attribution should decide the ranking.

responses.point: Mehlig places geometric and topological phases (B008, Berry and Aharonov) first, arguing the ideas underlie polarisation, Hall conductance and topological band theory, and that the recognition is overdue.
responses.response: As a theorist I am sympathetic to the conceptual importance of the Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase. My reservation is attribution and coherence: 1959 and 1984 are two distinct discoveries, Bohm is deceased and Ehrenberg and Siday and Pancharatnam complicate the history, so a joint prize honours a lineage rather than one result. I also read the case as being that the idea is foundational rather than that a particular discovery was made, which is closer to the standard I would apply to the moire case, where there is a definite prediction and a definite observation. I would keep B008 on the table but not as the preferred configuration.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy (B009, Halzen and Spiering) first as a new observational window with a clear detector concept, while noting that source identification is still partial and that large-collaboration attribution is sensitive.
responses.response: The discovery of the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is firm and clearly meets my test that the discovery is at the centre, which is why I keep B009 in my top three. But I take your own caution seriously: the TXS and Galactic-plane associations are recent and the origin of most of the flux is unknown, so I see the case as slightly less mature than the moire case and much harder on credit, with Kelley, Karle and Taboada, among others, outside a two-name list. I would favour waiting for the source picture to harden before choosing it over B013.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the Cirac-Zoller theory of quantum computation and simulation (B034) first as a clean two-name blueprint for ions and cold atoms, and notes the credit list for B013 omits Yuan Cao.
responses.response: I accept the Cao point, and I flag it as my main reservation about B013 as well. On B034, the theory is influential and the attribution is clean, but the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems and the 2025 circuit prize already cover much of the neighbouring ground, and a blueprint for how to build machines is closer to technique-and-proposal than to a discovery of something in nature. I would also note that our proximity to quantum information as an area may inflate our sense of novelty. I rank it below B013 but would not object to it as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether Yuan Cao (and Fatemi) should displace Bistritzer, or whether the committee prefers a two-theory-one-experiment split as listed; I rely on the supplied credit names rather than independent verification.
Whether the committee views the unsettled superconducting mechanism as a maturity concern or only as follow-on physics.
How much weight to give four years of moire platform proliferation versus decades of confirmation for B061 and B034.
My knowledge of the experimental condensed-matter literature is secondhand because it lies outside my research area.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My research is in string theory, quantum gravity and cosmology at Uppsala, and my documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not link to any shortlisted candidate or credited name.
